gdp-circular-flow-s2.title: From wheat to a loaf of bread
gdp-circular-flow-s2.html: In Country X a farmer grows wheat and sells it to a mill for $50. The mill grinds it into flour and sells the flour to a bakery for $120. The bakery bakes bread and sells all of it to shoppers for $300. Nothing else is produced along this chain this year.

gdp-circular-flow-s3.title: A week in a small town
gdp-circular-flow-s3.html: Lena works at a bike factory and is paid a wage. She rents a spare room in her house to a coffee shop that uses it for storage. On Saturday she spends part of her pay on a new bike from the factory and a haircut. The factory uses the money from bike sales to pay its workers, rent its building and pay interest on a loan from a local family.

gdp-limitations-s2.title: Three changes in Country Y
gdp-limitations-s2.html: Three things happen in Country Y this year. (1) Omar quits his paid job as a cook at a restaurant to cook at home for his own family, as much food as before. (2) A chemical plant leaks into a river, and towns spend millions of dollars cleaning it up. (3) A new law gives every full-time worker two more weeks of paid vacation; people work fewer hours and say they are happier.

gdp-limitations-s3.title: Cash work in Country Z
gdp-limitations-s3.html: In Country Z, many house painters, street vendors and tutors are paid in cash and never report the sales to the government. Officials estimate that this unreported work equals about a fifth of the output they measure. Country W, next door, has about the same production per person, but almost all of its sales are recorded.

unemployment-s2.title: Five people in Country Y
unemployment-s2.html: Ana quit her job as a nurse to move closer to her family and is applying for nursing jobs in her new city. Ben ran a printing press for 20 years; the plant replaced its presses with digital machines, and the jobs open near him need computer skills he does not have. Chen was laid off from a car dealership when sales fell during a recession; he is looking for work. Dee retired at 67 and is not looking for work. Eli lost his job a year ago and has stopped looking because he believes no one is hiring.

inflation-costs-s1.title: A one-year loan in Country X
inflation-costs-s1.html: Maya borrows $10,000 from a credit union for one year at a fixed interest rate of 8%, so she will repay $10,800. When they sign, both Maya and the credit union believe inflation over the year will be about 3%. In fact prices rise 8% over the year: the consumer price index goes from 100 to 108.

inflation-costs-s2.title: A surprise jump in inflation in Country Q
inflation-costs-s2.html: For years, inflation in Country Q was about 2%, and everyone planned on that. This year it jumps to 9%. Four people react: Ruth is retired and lives on a pension of the same dollar amount every month. Dev has a union contract that raises his pay each year by the rise in the CPI. Lucia owns a restaurant and has reprinted her menus twice to show higher prices. Tom now keeps less cash in his wallet and goes to the bank more often, so his money does not sit losing value.

business-cycles-s2.title: A slowdown in Arland
business-cycles-s2.html: In Arland, households and firms cut back on spending. For two quarters in a row real GDP falls, stores report weak sales and factories cut shifts. The unemployment rate rises from 4.5% to 7.0%. Economists estimate Arland's natural rate of unemployment at 4.5%.

business-cycles-s3.title: A boom in Berovia
business-cycles-s3.html: Berovia's economy is booming. Firms are running extra shifts and paying overtime, and some workers have put off retiring to take well-paid jobs. The unemployment rate is 3.0%, while the natural rate is estimated at 5.0%. Prices are rising faster each month.

items.q: Use the table. What is GDP in Country X, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: You added imports. Imports are subtracted: they are already inside consumption, investment and government purchases but were produced abroad.
You counted transfer payments. A pension check pays for nothing produced this year, so it is not part of GDP; it is counted when the money is spent.

You left out net exports. Add exports and subtract imports: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X - M = 80 - 100 = -20</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Use the table. What are net exports in Country X, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: The size is right but the sign is wrong. Net exports are exports minus imports, and imports are larger here, so the answer is negative.
You added exports and imports. Net exports subtract imports from exports.

items.q: Why is the $90 billion of transfer payments in the table left out of GDP?
options: No good or service is produced in exchange for the payment
The government pays it, and government spending is not part of GDP
It is counted later as part of net exports
It is too small a share of GDP to be worth measuring

items.q: Next year households in Country X buy $20 billion more of imported phones, and nothing else in the table changes. What happens to Country X's GDP?
options: It stays the same: the extra consumption is offset by imports
It rises by $20 billion, because consumption spending rose
It falls by $20 billion, because imports are subtracted
It rises by $40 billion, counting both the spending and the imports

items.q: How much does this chain add to Country X's GDP, in dollars?

mistakes.why: You added every sale. The wheat and flour are intermediate goods already inside the bread's price, so adding them counts them twice.
That is the price of the flour, an intermediate good. GDP counts the final good sold to the people who use it: the bread.

items.q: What is the value added by the bakery, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is the bakery's sales. Value added subtracts what the bakery paid for flour: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>300</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">300 - 120</annotation></semantics></math>.
You subtracted the price of the wheat. The bakery bought flour for $120, so subtract that.

items.q: A student adds <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>120</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>300</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50 + 120 + 300</annotation></semantics></math> to measure what this chain adds to GDP. What is the error?
options: Double counting: the wheat and flour are inside the bread's price
Leaving out the farmer's costs, which are also part of GDP
Counting the bread, which is a consumer good and not part of GDP
Mixing goods and services, which are measured in separate accounts

It rises by 2%, the same as the rise in GDP

items.q: Country V's GDP is 600 billion dollars and its population is 30 million. Next year GDP is 660 billion and the population is 33 million. What is GDP per capita next year, in dollars per person?

mistakes.why: You divided next year's GDP by this year's population. Use next year's population, 33 million.
The digits are right but the units were dropped: billions divided by millions gives thousands, so the answer is 20,000 dollars.

items.q: A smartphone today costs about the same as one did ten years ago but does far more. Which limitation of GDP does this show?
options: GDP counts the price paid and can miss gains in quality
GDP leaves out goods produced by firms based abroad

GDP leaves out goods that households buy for themselves

items.q: Two countries have the same GDP per capita. Which difference between them would GDP per capita fail to show?

One has twice the population and twice the total GDP
One produces more final goods per person than the other
One has a larger total market value of final output

items.q: What is the labor force in Country X, in millions of people?

mistakes.why: That is only the employed. The labor force also includes the unemployed, people without a job who are looking: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>150</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150 + 10</annotation></semantics></math>.
That is the adult population. The labor force leaves out the 90 million who are neither working nor looking.

items.q: What is the unemployment rate in Country X?

mistakes.why: You divided by the adult population. The unemployment rate divides by the labor force (employed + unemployed = 160 million).
You divided by the employed. The denominator is the whole labor force: the employed plus the unemployed.

items.q: What is the labor force participation rate in Country X?

mistakes.why: You used only the employed. The labor force is the employed plus the unemployed, 160 million.
That is the share not in the labor force. Participation is the share that is in it: 160 out of 250.

items.q: What is Country Z's natural rate of unemployment?

mistakes.why: That is the actual rate in Year 2. The natural rate adds only frictional and structural unemployment.

That is only frictional unemployment. Add structural unemployment too: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2 + 3</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: What is the cyclical unemployment rate in Year 2?

mistakes.why: You added the actual and natural rates. Cyclical unemployment is the actual rate minus the natural rate.

You subtracted only the frictional rate. Subtract the whole natural rate, frictional plus structural: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8 - 5</annotation></semantics></math>.

slips.PPC: More workers is more of a factor of production: the curve moves out, not in.

items.q: Ivy works 10 hours a week at a store but wants full-time work. How does the way she is counted affect the unemployment rate as a measure of joblessness?

items.q: Country V's labor force is 80 million and its unemployment rate is 5%. How many people are unemployed, in millions?

mistakes.why: You multiplied 5 by 80 but did not divide by 100. Five percent is 0.05, so <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.05</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>80</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05 \times 80 = 4</annotation></semantics></math>.

You divided 80 by 5. Five percent of 80 is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.05</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>80</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.05 \times 80</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: What does the market basket cost in 2025, in dollars?

mistakes.why: You added the three prices. The basket holds 10 pizzas, 20 gallons and 5 tickets: multiply each price by its quantity first.

items.q: With 2024 as the base year, what is the consumer price index for 2025?

mistakes.why: You divided but did not multiply by 100. An index is the ratio times 100, so the base year is 100.
The fraction is upside down. Put the year you are measuring on top: cost in 2025 over cost in the base year.

items.q: What is the inflation rate from 2025 to 2026, measured by this index?

mistakes.why: That is the rise since the base year (121 - 100). The inflation rate for one year compares 2026 with 2025.

That is the rise in index points. Divide the change by the starting index: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>11</mn><mn>110</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{11}{110} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: What was the inflation rate in Year 2?

mistakes.why: 104 is the index itself. Inflation is the percent change in the index: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>104</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mn>100</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{104 - 100}{100} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Rosa earns a nominal wage of <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">$30</annotation></semantics></math> an hour. The CPI is 120. What is her real wage in base-year dollars per hour?

mistakes.why: You multiplied by the index. Prices are higher than in the base year, so the wage buys less: divide by the index, then multiply by 100.
You divided by the index but did not multiply by 100. The index is in units where the base year is 100.

items.q: A job paid <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">$40{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> a year in the base year. The CPI is now 125. What nominal salary would buy the same goods today, in dollars?

mistakes.why: You divided by the index. To keep up with prices that are 25% higher, the salary must be larger: multiply by <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>125</mn><mn>100</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{125}{100}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Measured in the prices of the day Maya borrowed, how much is her $10,800 repayment worth, in dollars?

mistakes.why: That is the dollar amount repaid. Prices rose 8%, so divide by the index: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>800</mn></mrow><mn>108</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{10{,}800}{108} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>.

options: The credit union: repaid dollars buy more than planned
Maya, because her interest rate was fixed for the whole year

items.q: Build the explanation: households and firms in Country V cut their spending sharply. Explain what happens to output and unemployment.

spending.label: Total spending
options: falls
rises

why.1: Households and firms cut their spending, so total spending falls.

output.label: Real GDP
options: falls below potential
rises above potential

why.1: Firms sell less, so they produce less: output falls, it does not rise.

gap.label: The output gap
options: negative (recessionary)
positive (inflationary)

options: rises
